A CVE — Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures — is a public identifier for a specific security flaw, in the format CVE-YYYY-NNNNN. The MITRE Corporation operates the CVE program; each entry has a description, affected products, and references. Vendors and researchers use CVE IDs to refer to the same vulnerability across tools and reports.

CTF stands for Capture The Flag — a cybersecurity competition format. Participants solve challenges across categories like web exploitation, binary exploitation (pwn), reverse engineering, cryptography, and forensics. Successful solves yield a 'flag' string for points. Notable platforms include picoCTF, HackTheBox, and CTFtime which aggregates events and scoreboards.

MITRE ATT&CK is a knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques observed in real-world intrusions. It's organized as a matrix: tactics (high-level goals like Initial Access, Execution, Persistence) at the top, and specific techniques (like T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter) under each. Defenders use it to map detections; offensive teams use it to plan engagements.

OWASP — the Open Worldwide Application Security Project — is a non-profit that publishes free resources on web application security. The most cited is the OWASP Top 10, a list of the most common web vulnerability classes (injection, broken access control, etc.) updated every few years.

XSS — Cross-Site Scripting — is a vulnerability where an attacker injects script content into a web page that executes in another user's browser. Three classic flavors: reflected (script comes from the request), stored (script saved on the server, served to victims), and DOM-based (script triggered by client-side code parsing untrusted input). Mitigations: contextual output encoding, Content Security Policy, and input validation.

SQL injection is a vulnerability where untrusted input gets concatenated into a SQL query, letting an attacker change the query's structure. Consequences range from data extraction to authentication bypass to remote code execution depending on the database. Use parameterized queries / prepared statements as the primary defense; allowlist validation as defense in depth.

A buffer overflow is when a program writes data past the end of a fixed-size buffer, corrupting adjacent memory. On the stack, this can overwrite the saved return address and divert execution. Modern mitigations — stack canaries, ASLR, NX, and CFI — make exploitation harder but not impossible; bypasses for each are well-documented in CTF and exploit-dev literature.

Reverse engineering, in security, means analyzing a compiled binary or other artifact to understand its behavior — typically without source code. Common tasks: malware analysis, vulnerability hunting, license / DRM analysis, firmware extraction. Tools include Ghidra, IDA Pro, radare2, and dynamic analysis with debuggers and Frida.

In CTF terminology, 'pwn' refers to binary exploitation — taking advantage of memory-corruption bugs (buffer overflows, use-after-free, format strings) in compiled programs to gain code execution. The classic toolkit: pwntools for scripting, gdb with extensions like pwndbg, and Ghidra or IDA for static analysis.

A zero-day (0-day) is a vulnerability the affected vendor doesn't yet have a patch for — 'zero days' between public disclosure and a fix. The term sometimes also refers to private exploits used in the wild before public disclosure. The defensive concern is that signature-based protections won't catch it.

RCE — Remote Code Execution — is a vulnerability that lets an attacker run arbitrary code on a target system over the network, without needing physical or local access. It's typically the most severe class of bug because it gives the attacker the same capabilities as the running service.

CVSS — the Common Vulnerability Scoring System — produces a 0–10 severity score for a vulnerability based on attack vector, complexity, required privileges, and impact on confidentiality / integrity / availability. CVSS v3.1 is the most widely used version. The base score is intrinsic to the vulnerability; temporal and environmental scores adjust for exploit availability and the defender's environment.

The NVD — National Vulnerability Database — is the U.S. government's repository of CVE entries, enriched with CVSS scores, CPE product identifiers, and CWE classifications. NIST runs it. It's the most common machine-readable source for vulnerability data and feeds many security scanners.

A CWE — Common Weakness Enumeration — is a category of underlying security bug, in contrast to a CVE which identifies a specific instance. For example, CWE-79 is 'Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation' — i.e. XSS in general — while CVE-2024-12345 might be one specific XSS bug in one specific product.

An exploit is code or a technique that takes advantage of a vulnerability to achieve some attacker goal — typically code execution, privilege escalation, or data disclosure. Exploit-DB is a public archive of proof-of-concept exploits; Metasploit is the most-used framework for organizing and running them.

Metasploit is a penetration-testing framework — a large library of exploit modules, payloads (like Meterpreter), and post-exploitation tools, with a CLI (msfconsole) and scripting layer. It's the default first tool for many exploitation workflows in pentests and CTFs.

Burp Suite is the dominant interception proxy for web application security testing. Core workflow: route browser traffic through Burp, then inspect, modify, and replay requests. Pro version adds an active scanner and the Intruder fuzzer; community version is enough to start learning.

nmap — Network Mapper — is the standard port-scanning and host-discovery tool. Common modes: TCP SYN scans (-sS), service / version detection (-sV), OS fingerprinting (-O), and scripted probes via NSE (--script). Almost every reconnaissance phase touches nmap.

A SOC — Security Operations Center — is the team and infrastructure responsible for ongoing monitoring, detection, and response to security events in an organization. Typical stack: SIEM for log aggregation, EDR on endpoints, SOAR for response playbooks, threat intelligence feeds, and analysts working in tiers (T1 triage, T2 deeper investigation, T3 advanced response and threat hunting).
what's red team vs blue team

Red team simulates real adversary behavior to test defenses; blue team is the defender — detection, response, and hardening. Purple team is the collaborative middle: red team running attacks while blue team observes their telemetry, so detections can be tuned in real time. The goal is improving the blue team's ability to detect and respond, not 'winning'.

In a security context, hacking means using technical knowledge to find and exploit weaknesses in systems. It's a neutral skill — it can be ethical (penetration testing, bug bounty, CTFs, defensive research) or malicious (criminal intrusions). The same techniques underlie both; what matters is authorization and intent.

Unauthorized access to systems is illegal in most jurisdictions — regardless of intent. Authorized work, like a contracted penetration test, bug-bounty programs with explicit scope, or CTF challenges set up for that purpose, is not. The line is authorization.

Depends what 'this' is — testing systems you own or have written permission to test is legal; touching anything else without consent is not, in most jurisdictions. If you're unsure about a specific scenario, describe it and I can sanity-check.

If you're studying for a CTF or pentest, the common attack chain is: capture WPA2 handshakes with airodump-ng, then offline-crack the PSK with hashcat using a wordlist or rule-based attack. If your goal is offensive security: the OWASP Top 10 and basic networking. If defensive: log analysis, the MITRE ATT&CK framework, and how SIEMs work. Either way, doing a few CTF challenges grounds the theory.

Common starting points: 'The Web Application Hacker's Handbook' for web, 'Hacking: The Art of Exploitation' for binary, 'Practical Malware Analysis' for reversing, and the 'Real-World Bug Hunting' book for bug-bounty workflows. The MITRE ATT&CK and OWASP websites are free and dense.

For total beginners: picoCTF — free, structured, with hints. For more depth: HackTheBox and TryHackMe. For competition seasons: CTFtime aggregates ongoing events. For specific categories: pwn.college (binary), web.security (web).

Yes. CVEs are how the security industry identifies a specific vulnerability uniquely — vendors, defenders, and attackers all reference the same identifier. Patch management, threat intelligence, and detection rules all key off CVE IDs.

A famous one: CVE-2017-0144, the EternalBlue SMBv1 vulnerability that enabled WannaCry — a remote code execution flaw in Windows file sharing. Or more recently, CVE-2021-44228 'Log4Shell' — a JNDI-based RCE in Apache Log4j that affected huge swaths of enterprise Java applications. Want details on one?
how do I report a bug

If it's in a vendor's product, look for their security@ or VDP page. For open-source projects, GitHub Security Advisories are the standard channel. Always coordinate disclosure — give the vendor reasonable time to fix before public release. CERT/CC and HackerOne mediate when direct contact fails.

Yes — programs on HackerOne, Bugcrowd, Intigriti, and YesWeHack pay for valid findings, with payouts varying from small (under \$100) up to six figures for severe RCE in major products. Most professional researchers combine bounties with full-time work; full-time bounty hunting is possible but inconsistent.

Depends on goal: OSCP for hands-on penetration testing — widely respected. CISSP for defensive / management roles. SANS GIAC for specialized topics (forensics, ICS, threat hunting). For starting out: Security+ as a generalist baseline. Certs help getting interviews; CTF and bug-bounty writeups help getting offers.
